essay.q: Present the design, results and mechanism of the Bastani et al. (2025) trial: three arms, three parts of each session, effects on practice and on the exam, and evidence for the "crutch" mechanism. State three limitations.
essay.m: Hint: Turkish high school students, nearly 1000, four 90-minute sessions; control, GPT Base, GPT Tutor (hints not answers, solutions and common mistakes from teachers); randomised by class; practice part intervened on, closed-book exam; practice +48% and +127%; exam GPT Base −17% (−0.054), GPT Tutor no different (−0.004). GPT Base correct 51% (logic 42%, arithmetic 8%); errors did not spill over to the exam; students asked for and copied answers (67% vs 37%); overly optimistic perceptions; dispersion fell in practice but not durably. Limits: one subject, one school, short term, fall 2023; the mechanism needs further controlled experiments.

essay.q: Present the design and results of Kestin et al. (2025): the crossover design, learning and perception results, and the authors' explanation. State the conditions on which the results may depend.
essay.m: Hint: Harvard PS2, N = 194; two lessons in two weeks; AI at home vs in-class active learning; randomised by groups of 2 to 3 students; medians 4.5 vs 3.5; z = −5.6; effect size 0.63 (low) and 0.73 to 1.3 (quantile); median time 49 minutes; higher engagement and motivation; 83% found explanations as good as instructors'. Explanation: seven pedagogical practices, personalised feedback and self-pacing. Conditions: first-time content, understand-apply-analyse levels, a strong model, question-specific prompts written by instructors, quality videos, a structured framework; the authors do not presume AI always wins.

essay.q: Compare Bastani (2025) and Kestin (2025): design, control, outcome measures and what can and cannot be drawn from putting the two side by side. Give at least two context differences that prevent a direct conclusion.
essay.m: Hint: Bastani: parallel three-arm, no AI as control, unassisted exam counted in grades; Kestin: crossover, control is active learning, post-test does not affect grades. Can draw (design inference): the design of the AI tutor matters (no guardrails harmful; guardrails neutral or beneficial). Cannot: level, subject, scale, motivation to do the tests, first-time content and prompt preparation differ; neither study is on programming.

essay.q: Summarise the opportunities and six main risks in Kasneci et al.'s (2023) position paper with mitigations, and explain why the paper is not empirical evidence on learning.
essay.m: Hint: Opportunities: for learners (summaries, exercises, explanations, writing support, disabilities, professional training), for teachers (personalisation, planning, language, assessment). Risks: copyright, bias, over-reliance of learners and teachers, difficulty distinguishing machine-written work, privacy, cost and equitable access. Mitigations: human oversight, awareness of limits, critical thinking, verification, training, data policies, open-source models, fair access. Not empirical: it is a position paper; mitigations are proposals; many cited studies are pilots or content generation.

essay.q: Explain Holmes et al.'s (2022) argument that the ethics of AI in education cannot be reduced to data and algorithms; describe the three-focus preliminary framework and the risks of building a framework.
essay.m: Hint: Good intentions are not enough; distinguish doing ethical things from doing things ethically; three foci: data, computation, education (purpose of learning, pedagogy, role relative to teachers, access); overlaps and unknown unknowns; AIED is a design science aiming at behaviour change; ethics is not only preventative and the cost of inaction must be weighed; risks: stifling innovation, ethics washing, tick box; the survey is small (17 of 60) and the framework is a "strawman".

essay.q: Present the method and main findings of Jobin et al. (2019) and derive three concrete ethical design criteria for a thesis on AI for teaching programming (mark them as design inference).
essay.m: Hint: Scoping review of 84 documents (27 + 10 + 3 + 15 + 17 + 12); 11 principles; convergence around five (transparency 73, justice 68, non-maleficence 60, responsibility 60, privacy 47) but divergence in interpretation and implementation; geographic imbalance; non-maleficence more than beneficence; trust with a warning against excessive trust. Criteria (design inference): transparency (state AI limits and accuracy), fairness (check results by group), non-maleficence (measure dependence and scores without AI), privacy (conversation data), appropriate trust (Module 10). Limits: it describes documents and does not measure effectiveness; not specific to education.

essay.q: Propose a "responsible AI" model for a programming class based on all five sources, state the measurement design, and say clearly what evidence is still missing for programming.
essay.m: Hint (design inference): GPT Tutor-style guardrails (hints instead of answers, instructor-supplied solutions and common mistakes), Kestin's pedagogical practices (active learning, cognitive load, scaffolding, timely feedback, self-pacing), teaching recognition of hallucination and verification (Kasneci), principles of transparency, fairness, non-maleficence and privacy (Jobin, Holmes). Measure: scores without AI (as Bastani), appropriate reliance (Module 10), acceptance (Modules 11, 12), harms and flow (Module 13). No evidence yet: effectiveness in programming, long term, generalisation to Vietnamese students; the figures are from maths and physics.
